NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Three weeks after an apparent misunderstanding sparked a confrontation, deadly Hindu-Christian riots continue unabated in the remote east Indian state of Orissa. Police officers chase away a protester in Mangalore, India, Monday. By Tuesday, about 20 deaths had been reported, said Praveen Kumar, the superintendent of police in the worst-affected Kandhamal district. The latest casualty is a police officer who died after an armed mob of about 400 to 500 mostly Hindus torched a police station in the district on Monday, Orissa state police said. Orissa's Director General of Police G.C. Nanda the policeman died when the mob opened fire at officers fleeing the burning building. The attack, he said, may have been in retaliation for arrests that police made in the ongoing communal fighting.  Watch more about the riots in India » . The attack came two days after police fired on a crowd to prevent it from attacking Christian residents. Between three and six people died in the shooting, CNN's sister network CNN-IBN reported. The violence spread to southern India over the weekend when vandals attacked 14 churches in an hour in the state of Karnataka Sunday, the network said. The Christian community in the Karnataka -- numbering about 2.5 million -- said right-wing Hindus are targeting them for opposing the violence in Orissa. By Tuesday, police had arrested about 140 people in connection with the riots, said Karnataka's Inspector General of Police A.M. Prasad. Sixty of them -- all Hindus -- were arrested for the church attacks, Prasad said. The rest, mostly Christians, were charged with disturbing the peace, he said. Orissa has historically been a tinderbox of Hindu-Christian tensions. Some Hindu groups view the work of Christian missionaries in the state with suspicion. They accuse missionaries of bribing or forcing Hindus into converting. The seeds for the current conflict were planted on August 23, when Hindu leader, Laxmananda Saraswati, and four others were killed in Kandhamal after 20 to 30 gunmen barged into a Hindu school and began shooting, the Orissa chief minister's office said. The authorities have not determined who killed Saraswati, but after the incident they detained five people who are Christians, said Sukanta Panda, spokesman for the chief minister. The government says the killings may have been the work of Maoist rebels -- investigators have many unanswered questions -- but some hardline Hindus blamed a Christian minority. They took to the streets in anger, rampaging through predominantly Christian neighborhoods, ransacking shops and torching houses. They chopped down trees to block roads, making it difficult for police to reach trouble spots. A Christian orphanage was set on fire. A 20-year-old woman, who was teaching children inside, burned to death. Christian residents fought back, and the clashes spread. Authorities imposed a night curfew in many towns and deployed state and federal forces in the troubled areas, Kumar -- the police superintendent -- said. Both sides said the violence has left Christian churches and Hindu temples razed to the ground. This is not the first time the simmering anger has boiled over in the state with deadly consequences. In 1999, a Hindu mob burned to death an Australian missionary, Graham Staines, and his two children while they slept inside their car. And last Christmas, clashing groups killed four people and burned several churches in the same Orissa district -- Kandhamal. Maoist rebels, who claim to be fighting for the poor and the dispossessed, have been battling the Indian government in an insurgency that has resulted in thousands of casualties since the late 1960s. Some Christians accept the Maoist theory, saying the rebels have also struck against hard-line Hindus because they associate them as being closely aligned with the government. But Hindu groups insists that Christians were behind Saraswati's death. Unlike Orissa, Karnataka has until now been spared the large-scale clash between Christians and Hindus. But now, many in the Christian community fear their calm and prosperous state may become another battleground between the two religions, CNN-IBN said. CNN's Harmeet Singh contributed to this report .

**NEW DELHI, India (CNN)** — Three weeks after a fatal misunderstanding ignited a sectarian confrontation, deadly Hindu-Christian riots continue unabated in the remote eastern Indian state of Orissa. On Monday, police officers in Mangalore were seen dispersing protesters as unrest spread. By Tuesday, approximately 20 fatalities had been reported, according to Praveen Kumar, the police superintendent of Kandhamal, the district hardest hit by the violence.

The latest casualty was a police officer killed on Monday after an armed mob of 400 to 500 predominantly Hindu rioters set fire to a local police station, state authorities reported. Orissa’s Director General of Police, G.C. Nanda, stated that the officer died when the mob opened fire on police personnel fleeing the burning building. Nanda suggested the attack may have been retaliatory, triggered by recent arrests made in connection with the ongoing communal violence.

This assault occurred two days after police opened fire on a crowd to protect Christian residents from an impending attack, resulting in three to six fatalities, according to CNN sister network CNN-IBN. By the weekend, the violence had spilled into southern India, where vandals targeted 14 churches within a single hour in Karnataka state on Sunday, the network reported. Members of Karnataka’s Christian population—comprising roughly 2.5 million people—asserted that right-wing Hindu groups are targeting them in retribution for their vocal opposition to the violence in Orissa.

By Tuesday, law enforcement had detained approximately 140 individuals in connection with the unrest, according to Karnataka’s Inspector General of Police, A.M. Prasad. Of those detained, 60—all Hindus—were arrested specifically for the attacks on churches, while the remaining detainees, predominantly Christians, were charged with disturbing the peace.

Historically, Orissa has been a volatile flashpoint for Hindu-Christian tensions. Certain Hindu factions view missionary activities in the state with deep suspicion, alleging that missionaries use financial inducements or coercion to convert Hindus to Christianity.

The catalyst for the current wave of violence occurred on August 23, when Hindu leader Laxmananda Saraswati and four associates were killed in Kandhamal after 20 to 30 gunmen stormed a Hindu school and opened fire, according to the Orissa Chief Minister’s office. While authorities have yet to conclusively identify the perpetrators, five Christians were detained following the incident, said Sukanta Panda, a spokesman for the Chief Minister. 

Although the government suggested that Maoist insurgents might be responsible—noting that investigators still face numerous unanswered questions—hardline Hindu groups immediately blamed the Christian minority. Outraged mobs took to the streets, rampaging through predominantly Christian neighborhoods, ransacking businesses, and setting fire to homes. To impede law enforcement responses, rioters felled trees to barricade roadways. In one horrific incident, an attack on a Christian orphanage resulted in the death of a 20-year-old teacher, who burned to death inside the building. As Christian residents fought back, the clashes rapidly escalated.

In response, authorities imposed night curfews across several towns and deployed state and federal security forces to the affected regions, Superintendent Kumar confirmed. Representatives from both communities reported that the clashes have reduced both Christian churches and Hindu temples to ashes. 

This deadly escalation reflects a long-standing history of sectarian violence in the state. In 1999, an Australian missionary, Graham Staines, and his two young sons were burned to death in their vehicle by a Hindu mob. More recently, during the previous Christmas season, sectarian clashes in Kandhamal claimed four lives and left several churches destroyed.

Maoist insurgents, who purport to fight for the impoverished and disenfranchised, have waged an armed rebellion against the Indian government since the late 1960s, resulting in thousands of casualties. Some within the Christian community lend credence to the theory of Maoist involvement, suggesting the rebels targeted hardline Hindu leaders due to their perceived alignment with the government. However, Hindu groups remain steadfast in their belief that Christians orchestrated Saraswati’s death. 

Unlike Orissa, Karnataka had previously been spared widespread religious conflict. However, local Christian leaders now express deep concern that their stable, prosperous state may become the next battleground for interfaith violence, CNN-IBN reported.

*CNN's Harmeet Singh contributed to this report.*

**Title: New Delhi: The Beating Heart of India**

**New Delhi**, the vibrant capital of **India**, is a dynamic metropolis where centuries of grand history seamlessly intertwine with the soaring ambitions of a modern superpower. More than just the political epicenter of the country, it is a city of striking contrasts, rich sensory experiences, and undeniable cultural depth.

To truly understand **New Delhi**, one must appreciate its unique position in **India’s** story. Designed in the early 20th century by British architects Sir Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker, the city was built as a majestic imperial capital. Broad, tree-lined avenues, grand boulevards, and imposing neoclassical architecture set **New Delhi** apart from the winding, chaotic alleyways of neighboring Old Delhi. Yet, beneath this planned urban landscape lie the layers of ancient empires—from the Delhi Sultanate to the Mughals—that ruled from this strategic region for hundreds of years.

At the heart of **New Delhi’s** identity is its role as the center of governance for the world's most populous democracy. The broad expanse of Kartavya Path leads up to the majestic Rashtrapati Bhavan (the Presidential Estate) and the newly built Parliament House, standing as modern symbols of **India’s** political strength. Nearby, the towering arch of India Gate stands as a poignant war memorial, surrounded by lush lawns where locals gather in the evenings to enjoy ice cream and the warm night air.

Beyond its political significance, **New Delhi** is a sanctuary for history and culture. Within its boundaries, ancient ruins coexist with modern life. The towering, 800-year-old sandstone spire of the Qutub Minar rises above peaceful manicured gardens, while the stunning Mughal-style architecture of Humayun’s Tomb offers a quiet glimpse into the past. In contrast, the Lotus Temple, with its striking petal-shaped design, represents the city’s openness to contemporary architectural marvels and spiritual harmony.

No exploration of **New Delhi** is complete without immersing oneself in its incredible culinary and market scene. The city is world-famous for its food culture, reflecting the diverse flavors of **India**. From sizzling street food stalls serving crispy *golgappas* and buttery *parathas* to upscale restaurants offering refined regional cuisines, the city is a paradise for food lovers. Shopping districts like Connaught Place, with its white colonnades, and the trendy boutiques of Khan Market offer a taste of the city’s modern, cosmopolitan lifestyle.

Today, **New Delhi** is a city on the move. Powered by an advanced metro network, a rapidly growing tech and business ecosystem, and a thriving contemporary arts scene, it reflects the energy of contemporary **India**. It is a city where the past is never truly lost, the present is fast-paced, and the future is continuously being written.

**CNN.com**  
**SPECIAL REPORT: FAITH AND FRACTURE**

### Waves of Communal Violence Target Christian Communities in Eastern and Southern India

**By Sara Sidner and Mallika Kapur, CNN**  
*Updated 1430 GMT (2230 HKT) September 22, 2008*

**NEW DELHI, India (CNN)** — Flames of sectarian violence are spreading across parts of India, leaving dozens dead, thousands displaced, and raising urgent questions about religious freedom in the world’s largest democracy. 

What began late last month as targeted attacks in the eastern state of Orissa (now Odisha) has expanded south into Karnataka, where police have clashed with protesters following a series of attacks on churches and Christian institutions.

Federal authorities in New Delhi have dispatched thousands of paramilitary troops to restore order, but local community leaders say a deep sense of fear persists.

---

### Epicenter in Kandhamal

The wave of violence erupted in Orissa’s rural, densely forested Kandhamal district following the August 23 assassination of Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati, a high-profile leader of the right-wing Hindu group Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), along with four of his associates.

Although Maoist rebels claimed responsibility for the killing, hardline Hindu nationalist groups blamed the local Christian minority. Within hours, retaliatory attacks swept through villages across the region.

"They came with sticks, axes, and kerosene," said Father Thomas, a local Catholic priest who fled into the surrounding jungles with members of his congregation. "Churches were set on fire, homes were destroyed. People had to run for their lives in the middle of the night."

According to official government statistics, at least 38 people have been killed in Orissa, though independent human rights organizations estimate the true toll could be significantly higher. More than 1,400 homes and dozens of churches have been burned to the ground. 

Aid agencies report that more than 20,000 people are currently living in overcrowded government-run relief camps, while thousands more remain hiding in nearby forests, too terrified to return to their villages.

---

### Violence Spreads South to Karnataka

As authorities struggled to contain the crisis in Orissa, fresh violence flared hundreds of miles to the south in Karnataka. Over the past week, mobs targeted churches, prayer halls, and Christian-run schools, primarily in the coastal city of Mangalore and surrounding districts.

Hardline Hindu groups, including the Bajrang Dal, have openly admitted involvement in some of the protests, alleging that Christian evangelical groups in the state were engaging in "forced conversions" of low-caste Hindus—a claim strongly denied by local church leaders.

"We have never used force or monetary incentives to convert anyone," said Archbishop Bernard Moras in Bangalore. "These attacks are unprovoked and a direct assault on our constitutional right to practice our faith freely."

Images from Mangalore over the weekend showed police firing teargas and using batons to disperse crowds of both Christian protestors demonstrating against the church attacks and right-wing Hindu activists shouting nationalist slogans.

---

### Political Fallout and International Concern

The escalating crisis has put intense pressure on India's federal government, led by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. Speaking to reporters in New Delhi, Singh described the violence in Orissa as a "national shame" and vowed that perpetrators would be brought to justice.

"India’s secular fabric is the foundation of our republic," Singh said in a statement. "The central government will not tolerate the targeted harassment of any minority community."

The violence has also drawn international condemnation. Pope Benedict XVI called for an immediate end to the attacks, urging local authorities to protect religious minorities, while human rights groups including Amnesty International have called for independent inquiries into the response of state police forces, which some critics accuse of being slow to intervene.

---

### A Test for India’s Secular Promise

For decades, India has taken pride in its identity as a secular democracy where diverse ethnic and religious groups coexist. Christians make up roughly 2.3 percent of India's 1.1 billion population, living alongside a Hindu majority of over 80 percent, as well as sizable Muslim, Sikh, and Buddhist populations.

However, analysts warn that long-standing social and economic tensions, exacerbated by political mobilization along religious lines, are putting that secular promise to a severe test.

On the ground in Kandhamal, security forces are conducting sweeps to confiscate illegal weapons and enforce curfews, but for the thousands huddled in relief camps, the path home remains fraught with uncertainty.

"The buildings can be rebuilt," said one displaced resident in Orissa, holding her young child inside a makeshift tent. "But the trust between neighbors—that will take a very long time to repair."

---
*CNN's Harmeet Shah Singh contributed to this report from New Delhi.*

counterfactuals.output:
The **2008 Kandhamal violence** in the eastern Indian state of Odisha (formerly Orissa) remains one of the most severe episodes of anti-Christian communal violence in modern Indian history. Spanning several months starting in late August 2008, the riots resulted in widespread loss of life, mass displacement, sexual violence, and the destruction of hundreds of churches and thousands of homes.

Below is a detailed summary of the violence, its historical context, the trigger event, its spread to other states such as Karnataka, and its aftermath.

---

### 1. Historical Context and Pre-existing Tensions

The Kandhamal district is a remote, forested region in central Odisha populated mainly by two communities:
*   **Kandhas:** An indigenous Scheduled Tribe (ST) community, predominantly Hindu or animist.
*   **Panas:** A Scheduled Caste (SC) Dalit community, a significant portion of whom had converted to Christianity over several decades.

**Key Drivers of Tension:**
*   **Socio-Economic & Land Disputes:** Tensions existed over land ownership and affirmative action benefits. Under local laws, non-tribals cannot buy tribal land. Many Kandhas felt that Panas (some of whom sought ST status based on claims of tribal origin) were encroaching on tribal land and benefits.
*   **Religious Mobilization and Proselytization:** Christian missionary activity in the region dates back to the colonial era, offering education and healthcare. In response, Hindu nationalist organizations—principally the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP)—began organizing in the region in the late 1960s to counter conversions and promote *Ghar Wapsi* (re-conversion to Hinduism).
*   **The 1999 Graham Staines Incident:** Tensions in Odisha had previously reached a crisis point in January 1999, when Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons (aged 10 and 6) were burnt alive inside their vehicle by a Hindu extremist mob led by Dara Singh in the Keonjhar district of Odisha. This event highlighted the volatile nature of anti-missionary sentiment in the state.
*   **2007 Christmas Violence:** In December 2007, communal clashes broke out in Kandhamal following disputes over Christmas decorations and an alleged attack on Swami Laxmananda Saraswati. Dozens of churches were damaged, setting the stage for the much larger explosion of violence in 2008.

---

### 2. The Trigger Event: Assassination of Laxmananda Saraswati

On **August 23, 2008**, Swami Laxmananda Saraswati—an 84-year-old VHP leader who had led anti-conversion campaigns in Kandhamal for four decades—was assassinated at his *Jalaspeta Ashram* along with four associates (including a female ascetic, Sadhvi Bhakti Mata) during Janmashtami celebrations.

*   **The Perpetrators:** The Communist Party of India (Maoist) officially claimed responsibility for the assassination. Maoist leader Sabyasachi Panda stated they targeted the Swami because of his anti-minority rhetoric and role in regional communal polarization.
*   **The Reaction:** Despite the Maoist claim, Hindu nationalist groups blamed local Christian organizations and church leaders for conspiring with the Maoists to kill the Swami. The funeral procession of Laxmananda Saraswati, which covered a long route across Kandhamal, became a rallying point for angry mobs.

---

### 3. The Outbreak of Violence in Kandhamal

Following the Swami's death, systematic violence erupted across Kandhamal and spread to adjacent districts.

*   **Targeting of Christians:** Armed mobs attacked Christian villages, burning houses, schools, orphanages, and places of worship. Thousands of Christians fled into the surrounding dense forests to escape the violence.
*   **Human Toll and Casualties:** 
    *   **Official Death Toll:** The Odisha government reported **38–39 deaths**.
    *   **Unofficial Estimates:** Human rights organizations, local civil society groups, and Christian bodies estimated the death toll to be between **nearly 100 to over 100 people**.
    *   **Displacement:** More than **56,000 Christians** were rendered homeless. Over 25,000 lived in government-run relief camps for months, while others fled to cities like Bhubaneswar or left the state entirely.
    *   **Property Damage:** Around **300 to 400 churches/chapels** and roughly **5,600 homes** across 600 villages were looted and destroyed.
*   **Sexual Violence:** The most prominent case involved a 28-year-old Catholic nun who was gang-raped by a mob in Kinujhangi village on August 25, 2008, while local police reportedly failed to intervene immediately.

---

### 4. Police Casualties and Challenges to Law Enforcement

The Odisha State Police and central paramilitary forces faced immense challenges in restoring order due to difficult geography, widespread logistics disruption, and direct attacks by both rioters and Maoists.

*   **Mob Attacks on Police Infrastructure:** Armed mobs attacked several police stations and outposts (e.g., in Phiringia and Gochapada) to prevent security forces from intervening. Police vehicles were ambushed, and roads were systematically blocked by felled trees to delay the arrival of reinforcements.
*   **Casualties:** 
    *   Several police personnel were injured in clashes while attempting to disperse armed mobs.
    *   The region was simultaneously a Maoist stronghold; security forces faced a dual threat. In related security operations and ambushes around that volatile period, multiple police and paramilitary personnel lost their lives to Maoist landmine attacks and crossfire as insurgents took advantage of the administrative paralysis.
*   **Critique of State Response:** The state government faced severe criticism from the Supreme Court of India, civil society, and international bodies for its delayed deployment of forces and initial failure to protect vulnerable communities.

---

### 5. Regional Spread: Attacks on Churches in Karnataka

In September 2008, the anti-Christian sentiment generated by the Kandhamal events spilled beyond Odisha, most notably into the southern state of **Karnataka**.

*   **The September 2008 Karnataka Attacks:** Over two weeks in September 2008, at least 20 churches, prayer halls, and Christian institutions were vandalized across districts including Mangalore, Udupi, Chikkamagaluru, Karkala, and Bangalore.
*   **Instigators and Motives:** Hindu nationalist groups, including the Bajrang Dal and Sri Ram Sene, claimed responsibility for some of the demonstrations. They alleged that non-denominational evangelical groups (such as *New Life*) were engaged in fraudulent conversions and distributing literature critical of Hindu deities.
*   **State Action and Controversies:** The police response in Karnataka drew widespread controversy. Security forces used lathi (baton) charges and tear gas against Christian protesters who had gathered to protect churches or protest the inaction of the police, resulting in numerous injuries and arrests of Christian youth. The then-state government faced heavy political backlash for its handling of the crisis.

---

### 6. Judicial Action, Convictions, and Aftermath

*   **Investigations:** The Odisha government set up two fast-track judicial inquiry commissions (headed by retired High Court judges Justice Sarat Chandra Mohapatra and later Justice A.S. Naidu) to investigate the causes and extent of the violence.
*   **Convictions for the Swami’s Murder:** In 2013, a fast-track court convicted seven local men (and later Maoist leader Sabyasachi Panda) for the murder of Swami Laxmananda Saraswati. 
*   **Convictions for Violence:** Special fast-track courts were established to try riot cases. Several hundred individuals were convicted of arson and rioting, including **Manoj Pradhan**, a sitting Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) belonging to the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who was convicted in 2010 for his role in the riots.
*   **Human Rights Concerns:** Rights organizations criticized the low overall conviction rate relative to the number of police complaints (FIRs) filed, citing witness intimidation and poor police investigation. In 2016, the Supreme Court of India directed the Odisha state government to re-examine 315 closed cases of violence to ensure justice for victims.

### Conclusion

The 2008 Kandhamal violence highlighted deep-seated socio-economic, ethnic, and religious fault lines in rural India. The incident severely damaged inter-community trust in the region, left tens of thousands permanently impacted by displacement and trauma, and prompted international discussions on religious freedom and minority protection in India.

**Tensions Escalates in Odisha’s Kandhamal After Sectarian Clashes Leave 3 Dead; Police Probe Maoist Link**

**BHUBANESWAR, India** — Fresh religious and ethnic violence erupted in eastern India’s volatile Kandhamal district late Tuesday, leaving at least three people dead and over a dozen injured, local officials confirmed. Authorities have clamped down on the region with strict curfews and heavy police deployments, while intelligence agencies investigate the suspected role of outlawed Maoist rebels in fueling the unrest.

The clashes broke out in the forested hinterlands near Baliguda, approximately 200 kilometers (125 miles) classic southwest of the state capital, Bhubaneswar. According to local police, long-standing disputes over land rights and religious conversions escalated into violent confrontations after rumors of a desecration incident spread rapidly through surrounding villages.

Mob violence quickly followed, with armed groups torching several homes, vehicles, and a community place of worship before security forces could reach the remote area. 

"Three fatalities have been confirmed so far, all resulting from violent altercations during the initial hours of the riot," said Inspector General of Police (Southern Range) Satyabrata Bhoi. "Over 15 people are currently receiving treatment at the district headquarters hospital in Phulbani. The situation is tense, but currently under control."

### Heavy Security Deployment and Digital Blackout

In response to the escalating crisis, the Odisha state government deployed eight companies of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) alongside state tactical units to reinforce local law enforcement. 

Authorities have imposed Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, prohibiting public gatherings of more than four people across vulnerable parts of the district. To prevent the spread of misinformation and provocative content, mobile internet services have been temporarily suspended for 48 hours across Kandhamal.

"Flag marches are being conducted in sensitive villages, and police checkpoints have been established at all entry and exit points of the district," IG Bhoi added. "We appeal to the public not to succumb to unverified rumors."

### Suspected Maoist Influence

Security officials are focusing heavily on the potential involvement of Left-Wing Extremists (LWE), commonly known as Maoists or Naxalites, who maintain a presence in the dense jungle corridors of eastern India. 

Preliminary intelligence reports suggest that Maoist cadres operating in the CPI (Maoist) Odisha State Committee circuit may have actively stoked local grievances to re-establish influence in an area where their operational capacity had been significantly degraded in recent years.

"We have recovered inflammatory literature and pamphlets at the scene that carry signatures associated with local Maoist fronts," a senior counter-insurgency official speaking on condition of anonymity revealed. "It appears the insurgents are exploiting existing communal and tribal fault lines to create chaos, draw security forces away from counter-insurgency grids, and recruit disillusioned youth."

Historically, Kandhamal has been a flashpoint for ethno-religious friction, most notably in 2008, when the assassination of a prominent Hindu leader—an act later claimed by Maoist insurgents—ignited months of widespread communal riots that resulted in dozens of deaths and displaced thousands.

### Calls for Calm

Civil society organizations and local community elders have issued joint appeals for peace, urging residents to maintain harmony and assist law enforcement in identifying provocateurs.

State authorities have announced a compensation package for the families of the deceased and promised a swift judicial inquiry into the causes of the clashes and the security lapses that allowed the violence to spread. 

As night fell on Wednesday, security forces remained on high alert, with joint patrols searching deep forest trails for suspects involved in both the arson and the suspected insurgent orchestration behind the violence.

**SPECIAL REPORT**

### WAVE OF ANTI-CHRISTIAN VIOLENCE GRIPS ODISHA: POLICE STATIONS ATTACKED AND HUNDREDS ARRESTED AS KANDHAMAL BURNS

**By News Desk**  
**BHUBANESWAR, India** — A wave of sectarian violence targeting Christian communities in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa) has left dozens dead, thousands displaced, and entire villages burned to the ground. Centered in the remote, forested district of Kandhamal, the clashes represent one of the worst outbreaks of religious violence against India’s Christian minority in recent history.

State authorities have imposed strict curfews and issued shoot-at-sight orders in affected areas, deploying thousands of central paramilitary personnel to restore order as mob violence overwhelmed local law enforcement.

---

### The Catalyst: Ashram Assassination

The current wave of violence erupted following the August 23, 2008, assassination of 84-year-old Hindu leader Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati and four of his associates at an ashram in Jalespata. Saraswati was a prominent figure in the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) who had spent decades working in the region, actively opposing Christian missionary activities and religious conversions among tribal groups.

Although a banned Maoist insurgent group claimed responsibility for the assassination, Hindu nationalist organizations blamed the local Christian community. Within hours of the shooting, retaliatory attacks swept across Kandhamal.

Armed mobs carrying axes, iron rods, and kerosene targeted churches, prayer halls, Christian-owned businesses, and private residences. According to official estimates, over 30 people have been killed, though local civil society groups allege the true death toll is significantly higher. More than 3,000 homes and over 200 places of worship have been damaged or destroyed, forcing an estimated 50,000 people to flee into surrounding forests or government-run relief camps.

---

### Police Stations Under Siege and Government Arrests

As the violence escalated, state security forces found themselves directly targeted by enraged mobs. In several townships, rioters clashed with police to prevent them from protecting Christian neighborhoods or enforcing curfews.

In a series of coordinated disruptions, armed crowds attacked police outposts and stations, including facilities in G. Udayagiri, Tikabali, and Phulbani. In several instances, mobs surrounded police stations to demand the release of suspect rioters who had been detained, throwing stones and attempting to set police vehicles on fire. Law enforcement officials were forced to fire tear gas and live ammunition into the air to disperse the crowds, resulting in casualties among the attackers.

"The situation on the ground was extremely chaotic during the initial 48 hours," said a senior Odisha police official speaking on condition of anonymity. "In multiple locations, small police posts were surrounded by mobs numbering in the thousands. Security personnel had to balance restoring order with preventing the police stations themselves from being overrun."

In response to the breakdown of law enforcement, the Odisha state government launched a wide-ranging crackdown. Over 1,000 individuals have been arrested or taken into preventive custody in connection with arson, rioting, murder, and attacks on public property. Special investigation teams have been formed to track down ringleaders, while dozens of cases have been registered under the Indian Penal Code and the Arms Act.

---

### Historical Precedents and Socio-Economic Tensions

The 2008 violence did not occur in a vacuum; it follows a long history of ethno-religious and socio-economic friction in Kandhamal.

The region experienced a major precursor to the current crisis in December 2007, during the Christmas period. A dispute over the erection of a Christmas arch in the town of Bamunigam sparked clashes between Hindu and Christian groups. That outbreak resulted in three deaths, the burning of over 100 churches and chapels, and the destruction of hundreds of homes. Analysts noted that the 2007 riots served as an ominous dress rehearsal for the far larger wave of violence seen this year.

Underlying these clashes are deep-rooted socio-economic divisions. The conflict in Kandhamal involves two primary social groups: the Kandha adivasis (indigenous tribals), who are predominantly Hindu or animist, and the Pana Dalits (formerly referred to as "untouchables"), a significant portion of whom have converted to Christianity over the past several decades.

Tensions have simmered for years over land rights and affirmative action benefits. Under Indian law, Scheduled Caste (SC) status—which grants access to government jobs and educational quotas—is lost upon conversion to Christianity or Islam, whereas Scheduled Tribe (ST) status is retained regardless of religion. Friction has mounted over efforts by Christian Pana Dalits to gain ST status, which the Kandha tribals perceive as a threat to their legal protections and land ownership rights.

Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati had operated at the intersection of these tensions for over four decades, leading anti-conversion campaigns that amplified existing communal fractures.

---

### International Reaction and the Humanitarian Crisis

The violence has drawn sharp international criticism. The Vatican, the European Union, and the U.S. State Department issued statements expressing deep concern over the targeting of religious minorities and calling on the Indian central government to ensure the safety of Christian citizens.

In New Delhi, the federal government dispatched additional units of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) to reinforce the state police. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh described the violence as a "national disgrace" and promised federal assistance to rebuild destroyed homes and infrastructure.

Despite the heavy security presence, tension remains high across the district. Relief camps remain crowded, with many displaced residents expressing fear of returning to their villages without long-term security guarantees. Police patrols continue to enforce night curfews as legal proceedings against the hundreds of arrested suspects begin in special fast-track courts.

**Tensions Soar in Eastern India as Deadly Hindu-Christian Clashes Engulf Orissa**

**BHUBANESWAR, India (CNN)** — Violent communal clashes between Hindu and Christian communities have engulfed the eastern Indian state of Orissa, leaving at least 10 people dead, dozens injured, and thousands displaced, local authorities and media reported Tuesday. 

A strict, indefinite curfew has been clamped down across the worst-affected district of Kandhamal, a rugged, forested area that has long been a flashpoint for sectarian tensions. Security forces have been granted "shoot-at-sight" orders against rioters in a desperate bid to restore order, according to CNN’s sister network, **CNN-IBN**.

The recent surge in violence was triggered by the assassination of 85-year-old Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati, a prominent leader of the right-wing Hindu organization Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP), along with four of his associates at an ashram on Saturday evening. Although police suspect local Maoist insurgents were behind the hit, Hindu nationalist groups quickly blamed the minority Christian community, igniting a wave of retaliatory attacks across the state.

Over the past 72 hours, mobs armed with wooden batons, iron rods, and crude weapons have rampaged through dozens of villages. Churches, prayer halls, orphanages, and hundreds of Christian-owned homes have been set ablaze.

### Fleeing in Fear: The Christian Perspective

For the Christian minority in Kandhamal, who make up roughly 20 percent of the district’s population, the outbreak of violence has unleashed a nightmare of displacement and terror. 

Reporting from the region, **CNN-IBN** correspondents observed smoke rising over deserted villages as thousands of Christian villagers fled into the surrounding dense jungle to escape roving mobs.

"We were sleeping when a crowd of hundreds arrived shouting slogans," said Father Thomas, a Catholic priest from a village near Phulbani, speaking by phone from an undisclosed location. "They set fire to the parish house and church within minutes. We had no choice but to run into the forest with our children. We have no food, no shelter, and we are terrified to return."

Christian leaders have accused the state government of failing to protect vulnerable minority communities despite advance warnings that tensions were rising. 

"This is not a spontaneous reaction; it is a systematic targeting of our community," said John Dayal, a member of the National Integration Council and a prominent Christian activist. "Innocent people who had nothing to do with the Swami's death are paying the price. The police stood by as onlookers while churches burned."

### Outrage and Grievance: The Hindu Perspective

On the other side of the divide, Hindu groups express deep outrage over the killing of Lakshmanananda Saraswati, whom many locally revered for his decades of educational and social work among indigenous tribal populations.

Hindu leaders contend that the violence, while tragic, stems from long-simmering resentment over religious conversions in the region, which they claim are carried out by Christian missionaries using financial inducements—a charge Christian groups vehemently deny.

"Swamiji dedicated his life to uplifting the poor and protecting our ancient culture," said Radhakant Nayak, a regional spokesperson for the VHP. "His brutal murder has shaken the very soul of the Hindu community here. While we appeal for calm, the anger among the local people is a natural reaction to the constant provocation and illegal conversions being carried out by foreign-funded outfits."

Sujit Kumar, a local Hindu resident in Phulbani, echoed the anger over the Swami's assassination. "They killed an old man who was our spiritual guide," he told **CNN-IBN**. "We feel our culture is under siege in our own land."

### Official Response and Security Lockdown

State police officials insist they are working around the clock to bring the situation under control, though difficult terrain and road blockades erected by rioters—using felled trees and boulders—have severely hindered the movement of security forces.

In an official statement, Orissa Director General of Police (DGP) Gopal Nanda stated that additional companies of the federal Rapid Action Force (RAF) and Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) have been airlifted to the region.

"The situation is extremely tense, but we are taking all necessary measures to prevent further loss of life and property," Nanda said. "Over 40 people have been arrested in connection with arson and rioting. We appeal to both communities to maintain peace and not pay heed to rumors."

Police officials also clarified that early evidence in the Swami’s assassination points toward a pre-planned attack by armed Naxalite (Maoist) rebels, who had previously issued threats against the Hindu leader. "We are investigating all angles, but people must not jump to conclusions and take the law into their own hands," the police chief added.

### A Fragile Peace

As state authorities struggle to enforce the curfew, relief camps set up by the government are overwhelmed. **CNN-IBN** reported that over 3,000 people have already sought refuge in makeshift government-run centers, guarded heavily by armed police. 

India's Prime Minister has condemned the violence and the assassination, calling the events in Orissa "deeply shocking" and urging the state government to deploy all available resources to safeguard minority institutions.

However, on the ground in Kandhamal, trust between the two communities has been severely eroded. With fires still smoldering and thousands hiding in the hills, local observers warn that restoring true peace will require far more than police boots on the ground—it will demand addressing decades of deeply ingrained social, ethnic, and religious divisions.

--- 
*Reporting contributed by CNN staff in New Delhi and field reports from sister network CNN-IBN in Orissa, India.*
